scenarios.title: Give the puck carrier a quiet lane
scenarios.objective: Choose support space that does not crowd a teammate or hide behind pressure.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the +x end and gold attacks the -x end. Navy2 carries the puck up the middle. YOU are beside the carrier. Gold1 is on the other side of Navy2. The coach asks you to move to a quiet lane where Navy2 can see you.
cues: Gold1 is on the carrier's far side.

scenarios.limits: Static practice freeze. It does not prove a player's awareness or a completed pass. An adult may read the questions aloud.

questions.prompt: Who carries the puck?
questions.explanation: Navy2 is the carrier. YOU can help by finding a separate target instead of skating beside the puck.

questions.prompt: What should YOU change?

options.text: Leave the carrier a little room
Move where Navy2 can see you

questions.explanation: Separation and a visible angle give Navy2 more than one choice. Standing on the carrier removes room and a passing lane.

questions.prompt: Place YOU in a separate upper-side lane.
questions.explanation: This example separates YOU from Navy2 and keeps you in the same play. A different clear lane can be useful if it stays visible.

questions.prompt: Arrange a support move.

options.text: Move out of the crowded spot
Show a target and check Gold1

questions.explanation: Start by locating the carrier, create a lane, then check whether Gold1 has taken it away. Support is useful only when the current lane is visible.

questions.prompt: Gold1 moves toward your new lane. What could help?

options.text: Stay because Navy2 saw you first

questions.explanation: Gold1 has covered the first angle. A new angle can reopen a target for Navy2, depending on where the carrier and defender move.

questions.prompt: Why does a quiet lane help Navy2?
questions.explanation: A separate lane lets Navy2 see a teammate without two navy players sharing one spot. It can create a pass choice while leaving the carrier room to carry.

scenarios.title: Find the next player after a pass
scenarios.objective: Recognize the new puck owner and move to support the next play.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the +x end and gold attacks the -x end. Navy2 has just passed to YOU. The pass is complete, so YOU have the puck near the middle. Gold1 is between YOU and the attacking end. Navy3 waits on the lower side. The coach asks you to look for the next help.

scenarios.limits: The completed pass is stated in the briefing. The still picture does not show pass flight, timing, or a required next action. An adult may read the questions aloud.

questions.prompt: Who has the puck after the pass?
questions.explanation: The briefing says the pass to YOU is complete. YOU are the new puck owner in this freeze.

questions.prompt: Who can YOU look for next?
questions.explanation: Navy3 and Navy2 are navy teammates in useful parts of the picture. Gold1 is gold, so that player is pressure, not a pass partner.

questions.prompt: Place YOU where you can see Navy3 and Gold1.
questions.explanation: This keeps YOU near the puck while opening a view of the lower-side option and the defender ahead. Another controlled spot can work.

questions.prompt: Put the new-owner read in order.

options.text: Feel that YOU received the puck

questions.explanation: Know the new owner, notice the pressure, then find the teammate who can help. This is a read for the next moment, not a mandatory pass.

questions.prompt: Gold1 closes the middle. What might change?

options.text: Look lower for Navy3 or carry to room
Pass straight through Gold1 without looking

questions.explanation: Gold1 closing the middle removes one option. Navy3 or a carry may fit if that lane is clear; the new pressure decides.

questions.prompt: Why look again after receiving?
questions.explanation: The puck changed players, and Gold1 is ahead. A new look shows whether Navy2, Navy3, or open ice is the most useful next choice.

scenarios.title: Use the blue line as a meeting place
scenarios.objective: Use a named rink area as a shared practice target while keeping space and awareness.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the +x end and gold attacks the -x end. The coach names the nearby blue line as the meeting line for this activity. YOU have the puck just behind it. Navy2 waits beyond the line and Gold1 is below. The coach asks you to approach the line and find Navy2.
cues: The coach names the nearby blue line.
YOU have the puck behind it.
Navy2 waits beyond it and Gold1 is below.

questions.prompt: What rink area did the coach name?
questions.explanation: The briefing names the blue line as the meeting line for this activity. It is a landmark here.

questions.prompt: What should you see before moving there?

options.text: A rule that says you must pass

questions.explanation: Navy2 is the teammate to find and Gold1 is nearby pressure. The picture does not state a must-pass rule.

questions.prompt: Place YOU near the named blue line, away from Gold1.
questions.explanation: This moves YOU toward the named line while keeping some room from Gold1. It is a practice example, not a required landmark distance.

questions.prompt: Arrange the meeting-line read.

options.text: Move or pass when the space is clear

questions.explanation: The landmark gives the activity a shared place, but the players still decide the next safe move. Check both teams before moving or passing.

questions.prompt: Gold1 moves toward the blue line. What should you do?

options.text: Look for a clear side before reaching the line
Go there without looking because it is named
Leave the puck and skate away

questions.explanation: The landmark does not stay empty when Gold1 moves. A clear side may keep the activity useful while preserving puck control.

questions.prompt: How can a named line help your team?
questions.explanation: A named line gives YOU and Navy2 a shared place to look for one another. You still need to check Gold1 and the open space before moving or passing.

scenarios.title: Recover after the puck pops free
scenarios.objective: Respond to a loose puck after a failed touch by finding the puck, pressure, and support.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the +x end and gold attacks the -x end. A pass from YOU to Navy2 has missed, so the puck is loose near the middle. YOU are closest. Gold1 is coming from the upper side and Navy2 is below. The coach asks you to recover with a new look.
cues: The pass missed and the puck is loose.
Gold1 is above and Navy2 is below.

questions.prompt: Who has the puck after the missed pass?
questions.explanation: The puck is loose after the missed pass. Nobody controls it in this freeze.

questions.prompt: What should YOU notice on the way?

options.text: The old pass as if it finished

questions.explanation: Gold1 is pressure and Navy2 is a possible teammate. The old pass is over, so the new loose-puck picture matters.

questions.prompt: Place YOU near the puck with Gold1 in view.
questions.explanation: This brings YOU to the loose puck while keeping the approaching defender visible. Another nearby controlled approach can work.

questions.prompt: Put the recovery read in order.

options.text: Choose a safe touch or shield

questions.explanation: The missed pass creates a new state. Locate the puck, see both nearby players, then choose how to touch or protect it.

questions.prompt: Gold1 reaches the puck area first. What should you update?

options.text: Look for Navy2 and a safer next move
Assume the puck is still yours

questions.explanation: Gold1 arriving changes who may control the puck and where pressure is. Find the new owner and support picture before choosing.

questions.prompt: Why is this a new read after the pass misses?
questions.explanation: The puck is loose and the players are moving toward it. YOU must look again at ownership, Gold1's pressure, and Navy2's support instead of repeating the old pass plan.

scenarios.title: Leave the boards to show a target
scenarios.objective: Connect a named rink area with becoming available for a pass.
scenarios.briefing: Navy2 holds the puck. YOU wait close to the boards in the attacking end; Gold1 stands directly between you. In this small-area activity, try finding a passing window toward the nearby faceoff circle. Nobody has moved yet. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: Gold1 is between the current partners.
The nearby circle provides a named search area.

questions.prompt: What is between Navy2 and YOUR current spot?
questions.explanation: Gold1 lies on the straight line joining Navy2 and YOU.

questions.prompt: Which cues matter before asking for a pass?

options.text: The colour of a seat in the arena

questions.explanation: The source supports checking teammate location and pressure. The unseen seats are irrelevant.

questions.prompt: Move YOU away from the boards toward a clearer window near the faceoff circle.
questions.explanation: This example moves off the blocked line. Other open windows may work. A static line does not certify a moving pass.

questions.prompt: Arrange one way to become a target.
questions.explanation: This is a suggested support routine; timing and defender response still need review.

questions.prompt: Imagine Gold1 follows into your new window. What might help?

options.text: Stand still because the circle is always right
Ask for the same blocked pass

questions.explanation: The circle is a useful landmark, not a guaranteed correct position.

questions.prompt: How did leaving the boards change the passing picture?
questions.explanation: Explain the change in angle relative to Navy2 and Gold1. Another clear angle can be a reasonable answer.

questions.prompt: If Gold1 keeps the circle window closed, what can YOU do?

options.text: Move to another angle Navy2 can see

questions.explanation: The defender changed the named search area. Another visible angle can help the carrier if its lane is clear.

questions.prompt: What two players must YOU read after moving?
questions.explanation: Navy2 decides whether a pass is available, and Gold1 can close the new angle. Both positions shape the next read.

questions.prompt: Place YOU above the circle with a clear view to Navy2.
questions.explanation: This example changes the direct line and keeps the puck carrier visible. Another clear support spot may work.

questions.prompt: Why is the faceoff circle only a search area?
questions.explanation: It helps YOU and Navy2 orient, but Gold1's location and the passing lane still decide whether the circle is useful.
